doc_summary: Buck and Ryan Greenblatt propose meta-level adversarial evaluation: training red-team policies that fool an oversight process on proxy failures verifiable via held-out ground truth, to measure whether oversight is locally adequate. They argue this is more reliable than sandwiching and that alignment research should shift toward direct measurement and eval-based iteration rather than extrapolation.

items.claim: Prefers evaluation settings that are explicitly allowed to be recognisable as evals over settings that must be indistinguishable from deployment, because requiring indistinguishability would make constructing proxy settings far harder and the evaluation's validity does not hinge on it.
items.quote: Note that we aren’t trying to prevent our models from knowing that they’re in an eval. A lot of these settings will involve things that are clearly for the sake of evaluating a model’s ability to stage a coup.

items.claim: Prefers directly training the model to be adversarial (removing slack) over relying on observing natural behaviour, because a misaligned model can otherwise sandbag or behave well exactly where it knows held-out checks exist.
items.quote: a misaligned model might be able to sabotage a sandwiching evaluations by purposefully giving good answers in domains where it knows that its developers have access to held out information, and answer much worse in cases where it knows we don't have access to the held out information.

items.claim: Choose proxy failures that force the model through the same hard steps as the real failure and only differ by ending in an easily observable outcome, so success on the proxy implies success on the real failure.
items.quote: This is an example of a case where we can pick a proxy failure which basically requires the model to do all the same steps that it would have done for the real failure, and then do something visible at the end.

items.claim: Treats evidence as convincing when it comes from a ground truth source that is stronger than the overseer (more expensive oversight, held-out info), and judges oversight by the worst policies it fails to reject rather than average behaviour.
items.quote: We basically want to evaluate the oversight procedure by looking at the badness of the worst models that “aren’t rejected by oversight”

items.claim: Construct analogous test settings by finding a similar setting where you have strictly more information (sandwiching, backtesting) and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting of interest.
items.quote: pick a different field of math where you think it should be about as hard for mathematicians new to the field to know whether answers are good or not

items.claim: Distrusts extrapolating from non-analogous settings and from sandwiching-style results, since models may sabotage them; wants explicit accounting for the possibility that the model is gaming the evaluation.
items.quote: we should explicitly take into account the possibility that our models are sabotaging the sandwiching experiments to make us think that the oversight strategies work better than they actually do.

items.claim: Doubts that a negative result (inability to train an inconsistent or bad policy) demonstrates safety on its own; it must be combined with ground-truth-based evaluations.
items.quote: Note that even if you demonstrate that it’s impossible to train egregiously inconsistent models in a setting, you haven’t demonstrated that oversight is locally adequate—perhaps the oversight forces models to answer questions incorrectly in one particular way.

items.claim: Values eval-based iteration with direct measurement over long-range extrapolation, expecting crunch-time alignment work to be empirical and measurement-driven, and wants researchers to practice this now.
items.quote: I’m therefore eager for alignment researchers to phrase their techniques in these terms and practice the kind of eval-based technique iteration that I think will be crucial later.

items.claim: Run evaluations separately per use-case/deployment setting because failure modes and oversight difficulties differ between settings.
items.quote: We think it will probably make sense to run these evaluations separately for different AI use-cases, so that you can adjust the oversight process separately based on the problems identified by these evaluations.

items.claim: Accepts a common-sense 'I know it when I see it' adjudication of whether a red team demonstrated a real problem when formalization fails, rather than demanding a perfect formal criterion.
items.quote: it also seems plausible that we can just adopt a “I know it when I see it” approach to deciding whether the red team has exhibited a real problem.

items.claim: Open problem: formalizing the evaluation for recursive/multi-agent oversight setups and handling capability elicitation failures like exploration hacking.
items.quote: We’ve spent a couple of person-days thinking about how to formalize this, and we don’t think anything we’ve proposed is totally correct.
